title: Stack Frames (Stackframes), the Von Neumann Model (Von-Neumann-Konzept), and the Instruction Cycle (Instruktionszyklus)
summary: This unit reviews stack-frame prologues and epilogues (Prolog und Epilog) and examines the Von Neumann model, including its four functional units (Vier Werke) and shared memory for programs and data. It also shows how linking (Linken) and self-modifying code (selbstmodifizierender Code) relate to memory contents, and how the processor fetches, decodes, and executes instructions step by step.
keyFacts: The stack is located in byte-addressable main memory.
The stack pointer marks the current top of the stack; the frame pointer serves as a reference point for positions in the stack frame.
The prologue sets up the stack frame and saves any required values; the epilogue restores values and releases the stack frame.
The calling convention specifies which registers must be preserved; not all registers need to remain unchanged.
Compiler optimization with -O2 can change register allocation and instruction order.
The four functional units are main memory, the control unit, the arithmetic unit (ALU), and the input/output unit.
In the Von Neumann model, programs and data are stored in the same main memory.
Main memory consists of equally sized cells with consecutive addresses.
Instructions and data are encoded memory contents; instructions are encoded according to the ISA.
Instructions are generally stored at ascending addresses and executed sequentially.
Conditional and unconditional jumps can change the sequential order of execution.
Harvard uses separate program and data memories; one hybrid design uses shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches.
Write protection and splitting program and data into separate memories are different questions.
Linking combines program parts and libraries, resolves references, and adjusts addresses where necessary.
Self-modifying code changes its own program code and is now a rare exception.
The program counter (PC/BZ) holds the instruction address; the fetched instruction is loaded into the instruction register (IR).
The instruction cycle includes fetching, advancing the PC, decoding, determining and fetching operands, executing, and storing the result.
For lw, the instruction address and data address are different; the data address is the base register plus the offset.
The PC advances according to the instruction length; an instruction may be, for example, 2 or 4 bytes long.
In the loop example considered, the numbers from 0 to 9 are added, giving a result of 45.

questions.prompt: Where is the stack located?

options.text: In a register file separate from main memory

questions.explanation: The stack is an area of main memory and, like main memory, is byte-addressable.

questions.prompt: The ___ is at the start of a routine and sets up the frame needed for the computation.
questions.explanation: At the start of a routine, the prologue sets up the stack frame and any necessary saves. The epilogue dismantles the frame at the end.

questions.prompt: In the Von Neumann model shown, which units belong to the processor? Select all correct answers.

context.content:
flowchart TB
    M["Main memory"]
    subgraph CPU["Processor"]
        L["Control unit"]
        R["Arithmetic unit / ALU"]
        L --> R
    end
    IO["Input/output unit"]
    M <--> L
    M <--> R
    IO <--> L
context.caption: The units of the Von Neumann model; the processor is marked as a separate area.

questions.explanation: In this model, the processor comprises the control unit and the arithmetic unit. Main memory and the input/output unit are shown outside the processor.

questions.prompt: In the Von Neumann model, programs and data are stored in the same main memory.
questions.explanation: Shared main memory for programs and data is a defining feature of the Von Neumann model.

questions.prompt: Which memory organization characterizes the Harvard architecture?

options.text: Data is stored exclusively in the input/output unit
A shared memory for programs and data
Separate memories for programs and data
Programs are stored only in registers

questions.explanation: Harvard separates program memory and data memory. A shared memory is the Von Neumann organization described here.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about the general instruction sequence.

options.text: Instructions are generally stored at ascending addresses.
Conditional and unconditional jumps can change the order of execution.
Instructions are always executed in this order, without exception.
A jump generally changes the order in which instructions are stored in memory.

questions.explanation: Instructions are usually stored at ascending addresses and are generally executed sequentially. Jumps can change what happens next, but they do not reorder the stored sequence.

questions.prompt: The program counter (PC), called Befehlszähler (BZ) in German, contains the address of the current or next instruction and is abbreviated as ___.
questions.explanation: BZ is the German term for the program counter, abbreviated PC. The IR, by contrast, contains the fetched instruction.

questions.prompt: After being fetched, an instruction is loaded into the instruction register (IR) and then decoded.
questions.explanation: In the simple model, the instruction is loaded into the IR and decoded there before the operation is executed.

questions.prompt: Which unit performs arithmetic operations?

context.content:
flowchart TB
    M["Main memory: programs and data"]
    subgraph CPU["Processor"]
        L["Control unit: instruction cycle"]
        R["Arithmetic unit: ALU"]
        L -->|controls| R
    end
    IO["Input/output unit"]
    M <-->|Instructions and data| L
    M <-->|Data| R
    IO <--> L
context.caption: The four units in the simplified model

questions.explanation: The arithmetic unit (ALU) performs arithmetic operations. The control unit directs the instruction cycle.

questions.prompt: A program component calls `printf` from a library. Which task is part of linking?

options.text: Resolve the reference to `printf` and combine program components
Divide main memory into equally sized cells
Keep all register values in a routine unchanged
Decode every machine instruction again at runtime

questions.explanation: During linking, compiled program components and required libraries are combined. References are resolved and addresses may be adjusted.

questions.prompt: Self-modifying code changes its own program code and is considered a rare exception today.
questions.explanation: Self-modifying code changes its own program contents. It is described as a rare exception today.

questions.prompt: Before a prologue, `sp = 0x1000`. The prologue reserves 48 bytes with `add sp,sp,-48`. What is the value of `sp` afterward?
questions.explanation: In this example, the stack grows toward lower addresses: $0x1000-48=0x0FD0$.

questions.prompt: Before the prologue, `sp = 0x1000`. The routine then executes `add sp,sp,-48` and `add s0,sp,48`. What value does `s0` receive?
questions.explanation: After reserving space, $sp=0x1000-48=0x0FD0$. Adding 48 then gives `s0` its original `sp` value, $0x1000$.

questions.prompt: A loop starts with `summe = 0` and `i = 0`. While `i ≤ 9` holds, it adds `i` to `summe` and then increments `i` by 1. Select all correct statements.
questions.explanation: The loop adds the ten values from 0 to 9. Afterward, `i` has been incremented to 10, so the condition `i ≤ 9` no longer holds.

questions.prompt: What result does the code produce after the loop in `t0`?

context.content:
addi t0,x0,0
addi t1,x0,0
loop:
  add t0,t0,t1
  addi t1,t1,1
  addi t2,x0,3
  blt t1,t2,loop
context.caption: Register arithmetic and a conditional backward branch

questions.explanation: The loop adds the values 0, 1, and 2. Then `t1` equals 3, so `blt t1,t2,loop` no longer branches; as a result, `t0` contains 3.

questions.prompt: In the instruction cycle shown, which phase immediately follows decoding?

context.content:
flowchart TD
    H["Fetch instruction"] --> P["Advance PC"]
    P --> D["Decode instruction"]
    D --> V["Evaluate operand"]
    V --> O["Fetch operand, if needed"]
    O --> A["Execute instruction"]
    A --> S["Store result"]
    S --> H
context.caption: Simplified instruction cycle

questions.explanation: After decoding, the source of the required operands or the address to use is determined.

questions.prompt: A register `s0` contains `0x2000`. Address `0x1FE8` holds the word value 37. What does `lw a5,-24(s0)` do?

options.text: The value 24 is loaded from address `0x2000` into `a5`.
The value 37 is stored at address `0x2000`.
The value 37 is loaded from address `0x1FE8` into `a5`.

questions.explanation: The effective address is `0x2000 - 24 = 0x1FE8`. `lw` loads the word value stored there into `a5`; it does not load the address itself.

questions.prompt: A 2-byte instruction `mv` is at address `0x688`. What address does the PC point to after advancing for the next instruction?
questions.explanation: The PC advances by the instruction length: $0x688+2=0x68A$.

questions.prompt: After a 4-byte instruction at `0x684` is fetched, the PC already points to `0x688` while the fetched instruction is still being processed.
questions.explanation: After the fetch, the PC advances to the next instruction. The current instruction can still be decoded and executed afterward.

questions.prompt: A routine is expected to return an agreed-upon result after a subroutine call. According to the calling convention, what should the caller expect?

options.text: The agreed-upon result is available; which registers are preserved depends on the calling convention.
The frame pointer always contains the return address.
The stack frame remains allocated permanently.

questions.explanation: The routine must provide the agreed-upon result. The calling convention specifies which register values must be preserved; it does not require all registers to remain unchanged.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about prologues and epilogues.

options.text: The epilogue must set all registers to zero.
The epilogue can restore saved values and release stack space.
The prologue can reserve stack space and save required values.
The prologue releases the stack frame after the computation.

questions.explanation: The prologue sets up the frame; the epilogue restores saved values and releases the frame. Resetting all registers is not part of this.

questions.prompt: With `-O2`, a compiler must use the same register allocation and instruction sequence as with an unoptimized compilation.
questions.explanation: Optimizations can change register allocation and instruction order. What matters is the required behavior of the program.

questions.prompt: A computer stores its program and data in the same main memory. Select all statements that apply.

options.text: Program code and data are encoded memory contents.
Shared memory necessarily means every program section is writable.
In principle, the machine can change memory contents.
Write protection and the separation of program and data memory are separate issues.

questions.explanation: Programs and data are stored as encoded contents in memory, and memory contents can in principle be changed. This does not mean that every area is writable: write protection is a separate issue.

questions.prompt: A shared main memory with separate instruction and data caches is a hybrid design; it is not automatically the same as having two separate main memories.
questions.explanation: The hybrid design described retains shared main memory and separates only the instruction and data caches.

questions.prompt: A compiled program contains a reference to a function in a library. What can the linker do?

options.text: Advance the program counter during execution
Recompile the function every time it is called
Copy the contents of every data register into main memory
Resolve the reference and adjust any necessary addresses

questions.explanation: The linker combines program components and library components, resolves references, and adjusts addresses where necessary.

questions.prompt: After an instruction is fetched, the PC may already point to the ___ while the fetched instruction is still being decoded or executed.
questions.explanation: The PC advances after the fetch. Therefore, it can already contain the address of the next instruction while the current instruction is still being processed.

questions.prompt: For `s0 = 0x1000`, the data access `lw a5,-24(s0)` is performed. Which effective address is read?
questions.explanation: The effective address is the base register plus the offset: $0x1000-24=0x0FE8$.

questions.prompt: For an instruction `lw a5,-24(s0)`, `fe842783` is shown as machine code. What does this hexadecimal value represent?

options.text: The data value loaded from memory

questions.explanation: The hexadecimal value is the machine code for the instruction. The data value is read separately from the address specified by `s0 - 24`.

questions.prompt: Which address is used for the data access of `lw`?

context.content:
flowchart LR
    F["Fetch instruction at PC 0x684"] --> I["IR contains lw"]
    F --> P["PC becomes 0x688"]
    I --> E["Effective address: s0 - 24"]
    E --> D["Read data value"]
    D --> R["Write value to a5"]
context.caption: Instruction fetch and data access for lw

options.text: The address of the instruction register

questions.explanation: The instruction is fetched at `0x684`, but its operand is at the effective address `s0 - 24`. Instruction and data accesses use different addresses.

questions.prompt: A 4-byte instruction is at `0x684`, and the following 2-byte instruction is at `0x688`. What does this example show about how the PC advances?

options.text: The PC always advances by exactly 1 byte.
The PC always advances by exactly 4 bytes.
The PC advances by the length of the instruction.
The PC changes only after the result is stored.

questions.explanation: The first instruction advances the PC from `0x684` to `0x688`; the following 2-byte instruction advances it to `0x68A`. The step size depends on the instruction length.

questions.prompt: Because main memory is byte-addressable, `PC++` always means that the PC increases by exactly one byte.
questions.explanation: The PC advances to the next instruction. The step size depends on the instruction length, which may be, for example, 2 or 4 bytes.

questions.prompt: A processor performs internally optimized steps. Select all statements that are compatible with the execution model described.

options.text: Internal execution must always correspond exactly to a simple one-instruction model.
An optimization must not arbitrarily change the required behavior of the program.
The externally observable behavior of the program must be preserved.
A jump can set the PC to a different instruction address.

questions.explanation: Internal execution can differ from the simple model, but it must preserve the required externally observable behavior. Jumps change the address from which the next instruction is fetched.

questions.prompt: For a stack frame, use the mapping of local variables to offsets relative to the frame pointer `s0` given in the context. Statement: the running sum is at `-24(s0)` and the loop counter is at `-20(s0)`.

context.content:
| Offset relative to `s0` | Contents |
|---|---|
| `-20` | Loop counter |
| `-24` | Running sum |
context.caption: Mapping of local variables in the stack frame.

questions.explanation: The table assigns the running sum to offset `-24` and the loop counter to offset `-20` relative to `s0`. Therefore, the statement is true.

questions.prompt: A 4-byte instruction `lw a5,-24(s0)` is at PC `0x684`; `s0 = 0x2000`, and the word value 37 is at `0x1FE8`. Select all correct statements about the sequence.

options.text: The data access reads the value 37 from `0x1FE8`.
The data access reads the instruction code at `0x684` as a word value.
After the fetch, the PC may already contain `0x688` while `lw` is still being processed.
The instruction is first fetched from address `0x684`.

questions.explanation: The instruction is fetched at `0x684`, and the PC advances by 4 bytes to `0x688`. `lw` then reads the data value at `s0 - 24 = 0x1FE8` and writes it to `a5`.

questions.prompt: During a subroutine call, `jal` stores the return address in `ra`. A routine later makes another `jal` itself. Why must it save its original return address?

options.text: The second `jal` overwrites `ra`; without saving it, the original return address would be lost.
The calling convention prohibits nested calls.
The second `jal` automatically deletes the stack frame.
`ra` always contains the stack pointer rather than an address.

questions.explanation: `jal` writes the return address to `ra`. A further call overwrites that value, so the routine must save the address it still needs beforehand and restore it before returning.

questions.prompt: An instruction sequence begins with `lw` at `0x684` (4 bytes), followed by `mv` at `0x688` (2 bytes), and another `lw` at `0x68A` (4 bytes). To what address does the PC point after all three instructions have been fetched and the PC has advanced?
questions.explanation: The step sizes are 4, 2, and 4 bytes: `0x684 → 0x688 → 0x68A → 0x68E`.

questions.prompt: A computer has shared main memory for programs and data, but separate caches for instructions and data. How should this organization be classified?

options.text: As the specified hybrid design with shared main memory
As a pure Harvard organization with separate main memories
As an organization without main memory

questions.explanation: The hybrid design described retains shared main memory and separates only the instruction and data caches. This is not the same as having separate main memories.

questions.prompt: Before the prologue, `sp = 0x8000`. The routine reserves 48 bytes, sets `s0` to the original `sp` value, and saves `ra` at `40(sp)`. The running sum is at `-24(s0)` and the counter at `-20(s0)`. Select all correct addresses.
questions.explanation: The new stack pointer is `0x8000 - 48 = 0x7FD0`. The `ra` save is at `0x7FD0 + 40 = 0x7FF8`; relative to `s0 = 0x8000`, the sum is at `0x7FE8` and the counter at `0x7FEC`.

questions.prompt: A compiled program contains a library call whose target is resolved during linking. Is this resolution itself self-modifying code?

options.text: Yes. Every linker call changes the instruction currently being executed at runtime.
No. Linking combines program components and resolves references; self-modifying code changes its own program code.
No. Linking means only loading data from RAM.
Yes. Resolving a reference is a conditional jump.

questions.explanation: Linking combines compiled program components and resolves references. Self-modification, by contrast, means changing the contents of the program's own code.

questions.prompt: A general-purpose computer should be able to perform different tasks using the same basic structure. Which statement describes the role of the program?

options.text: The computer's structure must be rebuilt completely for each task.
The program controls the computer for the task at hand.
The program replaces main memory, the control unit, and the arithmetic unit.
The program specifies that input/output is impossible.

questions.explanation: The Von Neumann model separates the computer's structure from the specific problem: the program for a given task controls the general-purpose computer.

questions.prompt: A register `s0` contains `0x3000`. For `lw a5,-24(s0)`, which statement correctly describes the load?

options.text: The instruction reads the word value at address `0x2FE8` into `a5`.
The instruction loads the address `0x2FE8` itself into `a5`.
The instruction reads the word value at address `0x3018` into `a5`.

questions.explanation: For a load, the effective address is the base register plus the signed offset: `0x3000 - 24 = 0x2FE8`. `lw` loads the word value stored there into the destination register.

questions.prompt: What value does the loop produce at the end in `t0`?

context.content:
addi t0,x0,0
addi t1,x0,0
loop:
  add t0,t0,t1
  addi t1,t1,1
  addi t2,x0,9
  bge t2,t1,loop
context.caption: Adding 0 through 9 with a branch condition

questions.explanation: The loop body adds `t1` for values 0 through 9. After the counter is incremented to 10, `9 ≥ 10` is false, so the loop ends with a sum of 45.

questions.prompt: Select all correct statements about the simple execution model and its deviations.

options.text: A jump can affect the address from which the next instruction is fetched.
The PC/BZ contains the instruction address.
In the simple model, only one instruction is executed at a time.
Optimized internal execution may arbitrarily change the program's externally observable behavior.

questions.explanation: The simple model considers one instruction at a time and uses the PC/BZ for its address. Jumps change what happens next; internally optimized execution must still preserve the required observable behavior.

questions.prompt: A routine modifies the callee-saved register `s1`. What must it do before returning, according to the calling convention?
questions.explanation: If a callee-saved register is modified, the called routine must restore it. `s1` is one of the callee-saved registers.

levels.title: In Practice: What Happens Inside a Computer

questions.prompt: A recursive Sudoku solver has several active calls. Each must keep its own candidate index; values required by the calling convention are saved during a call. What is the purpose of a separate stack frame here?

options.text: It separates the memory areas for instructions and data.
It ensures that all processor registers remain unchanged on every call.
It gives each active call its own locations for local values and required saves.
It links the Sudoku routine to an external program library.

questions.explanation: Each active call needs its own state so the candidate indices do not overwrite one another. Stack frames provide storage for this; the calling convention determines which values must be saved.

questions.prompt: You compile the same C code once without optimization and once with `-O2`. In the debugger, you see different registers and a different instruction sequence. What is the most likely explanation?

options.text: `-O2` automatically changes the meaning of the C program.
The program was already linked with its library during compilation, so the machine code must be identical.
The calling convention requires all registers to have the same assignments in both versions.
The optimizing compiler may change register allocation and instruction order.

questions.explanation: Optimization can change how a program is implemented, for example by assigning registers differently or reordering instructions. The program's observable behavior should still be preserved.

questions.prompt: A routine reserves space for 12 local integers of 4 bytes each and saves two registers of 8 bytes each. Ignore padding and any other values. How many bytes do these contents occupy in total?
questions.explanation: The local values need `12 × 4 = 48` bytes, and the registers need `2 × 8 = 16` bytes. Together, they occupy `48 + 16 = 64` bytes in the stack frame.

questions.prompt: You are modeling a simple computer: the CPU fetches program instructions from the same main memory that contains the app's data. Which concept describes this?

options.text: Harvard architecture: program and data memories are separate.
Stack frame: each call gets its own local storage locations.
Von Neumann model: programs and data are stored in the same main memory.
Linking: references between program components are resolved.

questions.explanation: Storing program instructions and data in the same main memory is a central feature of the Von Neumann model.

questions.prompt: An app and its data are in the same main memory. The operating system protects the program section from writes while allowing the data area to be written. What follows from this?

options.text: The linker must relink the program section on every write.
Write protection and separating program and data memory are different properties.
The program thereby automatically changes its own code.
The computer must have a Harvard architecture with separate main memories.

questions.explanation: Shared main memory can contain both protected and writable areas. Write protection alone does not mean that programs and data are stored in separate memories.

questions.prompt: You initialize `i` to 0. A loop executes its body while `i ≤ 9` holds and increments `i` exactly once per iteration. How many times does the body run?
questions.explanation: The body runs for `i = 0, 1, …, 9`, which is ten values. Once `i = 10`, the loop ends.

questions.prompt: Your program calls `printf`, but the function is in a separately compiled library. When building the finished program, the unresolved reference must be resolved and suitable address information added. Which step typically does this?
questions.explanation: The linker combines compiled program components and libraries and resolves references between them. It may also adjust address information.

questions.prompt: A routine sets `summe = 0` and then, for every integer `i` from 0 through 9, adds the value `i` to `summe`. What final value does the routine display?
questions.explanation: The routine computes `0 + 1 + 2 + … + 9`. The sum of these ten values is 45.

questions.prompt: A rare specialized routine writes new instruction bytes at runtime to memory locations from which it immediately fetches further instructions itself. What is this behavior called?
questions.explanation: Here, the program changes its own instructions in memory. This is self-modifying code.

questions.prompt: In the simplified process, `lw a5, offset(s0)` reads data from `s0 + offset`; a 4-byte instruction advances the PC by 4 bytes after it is fetched. At `PC = 0x684`, you see `lw a5,-24(s0)` and `s0 = 0x1000`. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Instruction address 0xFE8; data address 0x684; next PC 0x688.
Instruction address 0x684; data address 0xFE8; next PC 0x685.
Instruction address 0x684; data address 0xFE8; next PC 0x688.
Instruction address 0x684; data address 0x1024; next PC 0x688.

questions.explanation: The instruction is fetched at `0x684`. The data address is `0x1000 - 24 = 0xFE8`; because the instruction is 4 bytes long, the PC then points to `0x688`.
